questions.explain: Every autonomous action is classified on three axes — impact radius (session/object/service/cross-service), reversibility, and urgency — which together determine which governance track it follows.
options: Impact radius, reversibility, and urgency
Cost, latency, and throughput
Owner, reviewer, and approver
Frequency, duration, and time of day
questions.q: What are the three taxonomy axes used to classify every autonomous action?

questions.explain: The taxonomy table maps ag_failover to the 'auto' governance track with max 1 per hour and immediate notification, while drop_table_ttl requires synchronous approval plus dual confirmation and a dry run.
options: Both require sync_approval
Primary failover is auto-approved with immediate notification; DROP TABLE via TTL policy requires sync_approval plus dual confirmation
Both are prohibited tracks
Both are auto-approved without logging
questions.q: Contrast the governance tracks for a primary failover versus a DROP TABLE via TTL policy in the chapter's example taxonomy.

questions.explain: The policy engine defaults to deny: with no matching policy it returns a sync_approval escalation with a reason template, and requires a dry run — the system never assumes an action is permitted.
options: It approves the action by default
It logs a warning and proceeds
No matching policy means default deny: escalate to synchronous approval with a dry run required
It retries the policy lookup until one matches
questions.q: What does the policy engine do when no policy matches an action request?

questions.explain: Urgent high-impact actions execute immediately with simultaneous notification and a 30-second veto window; async approval uses a 15-minute window where timeout equals approval; sync_approval blocks until a human explicitly approves.
options: All tracks require a human click before execution
Urgent actions wait for approval like everything else
Timeouts always cancel the action
Urgent actions execute immediately with a 30-second veto window; async approval uses a 15-minute window where timeout equals approval; only sync_approval blocks
questions.q: How do the four governance tracks differ in human latency?

questions.explain: Each log entry carries a SHA-256 hash of its content including the previous entry's hash (hash chain with a GENESIS start), UPDATE/DELETE are denied at the permission level, and a DDL trigger prevents schema alteration — verify_chain detects any tampering.
options: Audit logs are stored in a shared spreadsheet
Append-only table with DENY UPDATE/DELETE, a DDL trigger against schema changes, and a SHA-256 hash chain per entry verified by verify_chain
Logs are only kept in memory
Encryption alone guarantees immutability
questions.q: How is audit log immutability enforced at the database level in the chapter?
